subject: english
title: Structuring an essay that convinces
intro: A good essay isn't about big words — it's about a clear idea, laid out so a reader can follow your thinking and end up agreeing. Most essays that lose marks aren't wrong; they're disorganised. This lesson gives you a reliable structure for the whole essay and for each paragraph, so your argument lands.

sections.heading: The shape of an essay
body: Almost every essay has three parts. The **introduction** tells the reader what the essay will argue — its main claim, called the **thesis**. The **body** is a series of paragraphs, each making one point that supports the thesis, with evidence. The **conclusion** pulls it together and restates the argument in light of what you've shown.

The golden rule: **one main idea per paragraph**. If a paragraph is trying to do two jobs, split it. A reader should be able to sum up each paragraph in a sentence — if they can't, it needs tightening.

diagram.caption: The shape of an essay: a thesis, body paragraphs that support it, and a conclusion.

sections.heading: The thesis: say what you're arguing
body: The **thesis** is the single sentence that states your position. 'Homework has both benefits and drawbacks' is weak because it doesn't take a side. 'Schools should reduce homework because it harms wellbeing without improving learning' is a real thesis — it makes a claim you can defend.

Everything in the essay should support that one claim. If a paragraph doesn't help prove the thesis, it doesn't belong, no matter how interesting it is. A clear thesis is the spine the whole essay hangs on.

sections.heading: Building a body paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explain)
body: A strong body paragraph follows a simple pattern. **Point:** open with a *topic sentence* stating the one idea of this paragraph. **Evidence:** give a fact, quotation, example or reason that backs it up. **Explain:** say *how* that evidence supports your point and links back to the thesis. Some teachers call this PEEL (Point, Evidence, Explain, Link).

The step students skip is the **explain** — they drop in a quote and move on. But evidence doesn't speak for itself; your job is to show what it proves. That explanation is where the real thinking, and the marks, are.

example.problem: Write a body paragraph arguing that libraries help communities.
steps: Point: 'Public libraries give everyone free access to information, regardless of income.'
Evidence: 'A library card costs nothing, yet it opens up thousands of books, computers, and internet access.'
Explain: 'This matters because a student without a computer at home can still research and learn — the library removes a barrier that money would otherwise create, supporting the whole community.'
example.answer: Point → Evidence → Explain, all pointing back to 'libraries help communities'.

sections.heading: Introductions, conclusions, and flow
body: Open with a sentence that draws the reader in and narrows to your thesis by the end of the first paragraph — don't bury the thesis. The **conclusion** should not introduce new points; it restates your argument and leaves the reader with why it matters. Never just repeat the introduction word for word.

Between paragraphs, use **linking words** (however, in addition, as a result, on the other hand) so the reader feels the argument moving forward rather than jumping. Good flow is what makes separate points feel like one coherent case.

options: The single sentence stating your main argument
practice.explain: The thesis is the one sentence stating the position the whole essay sets out to defend.

options: This essay is about phones in school.
Phones have good and bad sides.
Schools should ban phones in class because they harm focus.
practice.explain: It takes a clear, defendable position and gives a reason — unlike the others, which state a topic or sit on the fence.

practice.q: What should a topic sentence do?
options: State the one main idea of that paragraph
practice.explain: A topic sentence opens the paragraph by stating its single main idea, which the rest of the paragraph then supports.

practice.q: In the Point–Evidence–Explain pattern, which step do students most often skip?
practice.explain: Writers often give evidence and stop, forgetting to explain how it supports their point — which is where the real analysis and marks are.

options: Restate the argument and say why it matters
practice.explain: A conclusion pulls the argument together and shows its significance; it shouldn't add new points or simply copy the introduction.

summary: An essay has an introduction (with a thesis), a body of one-idea paragraphs, and a conclusion.
The thesis is a single sentence taking a clear, defendable position; everything must support it.
Build each body paragraph as Point → Evidence → Explain — and never skip the explain.
Don't bury the thesis or add new points in the conclusion; use linking words so the argument flows.
